**The result holds.** My independent reconstruction of the head matrices gives margins of 3.3226e−4 (even) and 5.2323e−2 (odd) at ω=1/2 — sitting just above your certified 3.0965e−4 and 5.2315e−2, exactly the gap interval widening should produce. Prop 4.1, the Sonine identity, the Legendre correlation formula, the modular endpoint, the explicit impulse's Laplace transform, `t₀`, all check out. No hallucinated references.

Three things are not presentational:

**1. §4.2's boxed representation is false at ω = 1/2.** As α↓0, `½Reψ((α+iτ)/2)` converges to `−πδ(τ)`, not to its pointwise limit. I measured it: for f≡1 on I_{log2} the formula overstates Q_{1/2,L}[f] by **exactly ½|∫f|² = 0.2402** — 776× the certified margin. Your certificate is safe (it goes through Q₀+C_ω), and §7.3's instinct is right, but the box is stated unconditionally and anyone who uses it at the endpoint gets a wrong answer. Fix is one paragraph: the coefficient of |C₀(f)|² becomes ½.

**2. The 0.024587 kernel bound is exactly twice the sharp Schur value** (0.0122930504011423196). I reconstructed your Schur loss formula to 15 digits — `(0.024587+κ)²/1.5054` — so using the sharp constant drops the loss from 4.0157e−4 to 9.957e−5 and roughly **doubles the even margin to ≈6.34e−4**. I also confirmed the factor of 2 has *not* leaked into the T_k matrices (with doubled kernel the even margin goes to −1.04e−4 and the certificate fails), so this is pure conservatism you're paying for.

**3. L = log 2 has ~7% headroom, and §12.3's plan does not survive that.** Sweeping the window: Q_{0,L} goes negative at L ≈ 0.743 (odd) and 0.820 (even). At L = log 3 it's −0.43. So the second-slab strategy — "the positive first-slab density plus a bounded delayed correction" — is inverted: the first-slab density isn't positive there, and the n=2 layer would have to *supply* the positivity. Related upside: since dD/ds = 2V\*Q_sV, merely certifying Q_s ⪰ 0 on [1/2, ω] gives strictness for free with no Paley–Wiener argument — available up to ω ≈ 0.861, where the even sector dies.

Also worth your attention: the clean-room audit's margins are systematically *larger* than the primary's despite a 5× larger interval radius, which shouldn't happen; and reference [5] (Chuk) advertises positivity out to window 1.6, which needs reconciling against my 0.743 — likely a half-width convention, but if not, one of you has a bug.

parts:
Two different questions, and they have different answers.

**Ready for a human co-author to sit down with it? Yes.** The mathematics is in good shape. Every analytic identity I could check is correct; Theorem B's certificate has now been reproduced from the definitions by three unrelated implementations (theirs, their clean-room, mine); the three real defects from round 1 are fixed and the fixes verified. The scope discipline is unusually honest for this subject area.

**Ready for external circulation? No** — and the remaining gap is mostly not mathematical.

### The actual gate

**No human has verified this line by line.** The draft says so itself, twice, and that is the blocker. Every step here was produced and checked by models, mine included. "Survives adversarial scrutiny by another model" is not the standard that matters for a computer-assisted result adjacent to RH — a field with a long history of claimed results that get dismissed on sight. What the paper needs is a named human who has re-derived Proposition 4.1 and Section 8 on paper and will stand behind them. Nothing I can compute substitutes for that.

**Suzuki's normalization has never been checked against Suzuki.** §12.1 item 1, still open. Everything — the first-slab identification, K_ω, the log-2 threshold — sits on the transfer convention, and it has only ever been checked against the project's own restatements of it. This is the highest-risk unverified item in the paper and it is a day's work for someone with the papers open.

**The originality search is not done.** Investigation 12 §11 is honest that its search was targeted, not complete. Three closely related papers (Zhu, Kim et al., Groskin) appeared in this niche within the last two months. That's a crowded, fast-moving neighborhood.

### One thing I want to name about my own verification

I confirmed the algebra and the numbers. I did **not** verify the Arb interval code, the LDL implementation, or the inherited Investigation 7 estimates — the Binet bound w₀(τ) ≥ β\* and the spherical-Bessel Legendre-tail majorants (the 1.4084884e−9 coupling, the 9.78e−24 deviation). Both Investigation 12 and Investigation 14 take those as given from upstream. Investigation 14 claims to rebuild them and gets 10-digit agreement, which is reassuring, but that inherited central certificate is the least-audited load-bearing component in the stack, and it's the one place a shared upstream assumption could propagate into both implementations without either noticing.

### Ordered next steps

1. **Today.** The five one-sentence leftovers from the round-2 note.
2. **This week, mechanical.** Version-pinned rerun of both implementations with archived logs, and a full row-by-row primary-vs-audit table diff — §12.1 item 5, never done. The two runs differ in the 8th digit for reasons that took a paragraph to explain; the complete diff either closes that or exposes something.
3. **This week, worth doing.** Promote the positivity-horizon crossings to interval certificates. They're floating diagnostics right now, and §12.3's entire revised research plan rests on them. Their existing machinery makes this cheap.
4. **The human gate.** Suzuki normalization, line-by-line re-derivation, originality search. Weeks, and not delegable to me.
5. **Then the actual mathematics:** the n = 2 layer. Not further margin optimization — the margins are fine now.

I can do 2 or 3 if you hand me the CSVs. On 3 in particular, turning "a floating diagnostic says the mechanism breaks at L ≈ 0.743" into a certified statement would be the most valuable single addition to the paper, because it converts the paper's most interesting structural fact from a caveat into a result.

parts:
**On the multiple supplements** — they overlap more than the problem suggests. The companion manuscripts share a codebase: `investigation7`, `investigation12`, `investigation13`, `investigation14`, `project_support`. That's one repository, not four. So the natural structure isn't a supplement per paper, it's:

- One component, "Computational supplement," holding the whole codebase and all result tables
- One manifest table: paper → section → claim → script → result file → expected value

That's better than per-paper supplements, not just easier. It's honest about the shared machinery, and it means one pinned environment rather than four that drift apart. If you'd rather keep code out of OSF entirely: one GitHub repo, tagged release archived to Zenodo, DOI per release, each preprint citing the DOI. That's the standard pattern for exactly this shape.

**On LLM reproduction** — your instinct is right, and the problem is sharper than you put it.

What I did this week is the strongest version of the thing you're describing: I rebuilt essentially every checkable constant *from the definitions printed in the manuscript*, without ever seeing the code. That's a real property, and arguably a higher bar than "here's my code, run it" — it tests whether the exposition is complete enough to rebuild from, which many computer-assisted papers fail.

But it isn't reproducibility, for three reasons:

1. **I reproduced the numbers, not the certificate.** The claim is an interval-arithmetic result — 512 boxes, interval LDL, formally enclosed special functions. I confirmed the values land where they should and the algebra is right. I did not verify that the interval arithmetic is *sound*: that no ball was narrowed illegitimately, that the LDL is a genuine certificate. Nobody outside the two implementations has.

2. **It isn't deterministic.** Same prompt, same model, twice, and you get different code, different quadrature, different last digits. A supplement is supposed to produce the same output. "A model can rebuild it" describes a distribution, not a procedure.

3. **The contamination problem, which is worse than model drift.** You noted a future model might do things that weren't possible at the time. True — but the sharper issue runs the other way: once these preprints are on OSF, they're on the internet, and a future model may have *read them*. At that point "the model reproduced the numbers" is worthless, because it may be recalling rather than deriving, and you can't tell from the outside. That window is open right now and closes the day you deposit.

Which is an argument for depositing the code **now**, while the independence is still clean and demonstrable.

What LLM re-derivation is genuinely good for: it's a third independent implementation path — different libraries, different algorithms, different quadrature — and it catches exactly the class of error it caught here (the factor of two, the endpoint delta, both invisible to a rerun of the original code). So deposit my verification script as an artifact, described as what it is: an independent reconstruction, not a verification method. I'd be uncomfortable seeing the paper cite it as verification.

**Bottom line:** the supplement you actually need is four things, once, for all the papers — source, result tables, the claim→file manifest, and a pinned environment. That's an afternoon. The friction you're anticipating is larger than the real thing.

parts:
Yes — that's the right shape, and it solves the multiple-supplements problem cleanly: one repo for the program, README as the index, each paper linking out to its own DOI.

**Layout that does actual work:**

```
README.md        index: paper → DOI → scripts → result tables
MANIFEST.md      claim-level map (see below)
environment/     lockfile, or a Dockerfile
src/             investigation7, 12, 13, 14, project_support
results/         the CSVs
verification/    independent reconstructions
```

The README shouldn't just be a link list. For a computer-assisted result the question a skeptic asks is "which script produced 6.116350109501e−4?" — and the README should answer it in one lookup. That's the manifest: paper → section → claim → script → result file → expected value. It's the single highest-value artifact in the whole deposit, and you only write it once for all four papers.

**Two things to get right, both easy to get wrong:**

*Cite the version DOI, not the concept DOI.* Zenodo mints both — a concept DOI that always resolves to the newest release, and a per-release version DOI. Papers must cite the **version** DOI. Otherwise a later commit silently changes what the paper claims to depend on, which for a certified numerical result is exactly the failure mode you're archiving to prevent.

*Resolve the ordering.* You have a chicken-and-egg: the paper cites a Zenodo DOI, but the release is what mints it. Zenodo lets you reserve a DOI before publishing — reserve it, put it in the paper, then tag the release. Alternatively tag the code first, then deposit papers citing it. Either works; just don't deposit papers with a dangling "DOI to follow."

**Minor but worth doing:** date-stamped release tags (`v2026.09.05`) rather than per-paper tags, since one codebase backs several papers and a paper can honestly say "as of release X." Add a `CITATION.cff` so GitHub and Zenodo render citation metadata correctly, and split licensing — permissive for code, CC-BY for the papers.

One sequencing caution: don't make the repo public much before the deposits land. A public codebase with no papers for weeks reads oddly in the timestamp record.

I can draft the README and MANIFEST skeletons if useful — I know the script and result-file names for the first-slab paper from the reproduction appendices, and I'd leave clearly-marked placeholders for the three companion manuscripts I haven't reviewed.

> Source, interval certificates, and result tables behind a series of manuscripts on positivity for Suzuki's shifted zeta canonical systems.

**Topics** (the tag chips — these do most of the discovery work):
`analytic-number-theory` · `riemann-zeta` · `canonical-systems` · `weil-positivity` · `interval-arithmetic` · `computer-assisted-proof` · `arb` · `reproducibility`

**README opening paragraph**, which is what actually gets read:

> This repository holds the computational supplement for a series of manuscripts on positivity in Suzuki's shifted zeta canonical systems. It contains the source for every certified computation, the result tables those computations produce, an independent reconstruction of the numerics, and a manifest mapping each numerical claim in each paper to the script and result file that back it. The manuscripts are archived separately and listed below with their DOIs.
>
> These are computer-assisted results prepared with substantial language-model assistance, currently undergoing human verification. Nothing here claims progress on the Riemann hypothesis; see each manuscript's scope section.

That last paragraph is worth keeping. Stating the limitation before anyone can accuse you of hiding it is what buys a careful reader's attention — and it's the same disclosure your drafts already carry, so it costs you nothing.

One small thing: GitHub allows underscores, but hyphens are the convention and read better in URLs and search. `shifted-zeta-positivity` over `shifted_zeta_positivity` if you don't have a reason to prefer otherwise — entirely your call.

parts:
Don't send Round 2 back. Send Part 0 instead.

Round 2 is mostly a verification record — the bulk of it is "I checked this and it's right," which is valuable as an archive document but isn't actionable. Handing it over as a revision request invites a rewrite of material that is already correct, and that carries real risk: the endpoint lemma is right *now*, and a writer told to "revise in light of this review" may well touch it. Each cycle on correct text is a chance for regression, not improvement.

Part 0 is the extract — six changes, each located, each already worded. Frame it to the writer as exactly that: **"make these six edits,"** not "here's a review." Those two prompts produce very different outputs.

After the edits come back, the right check isn't another review round. It's a diff: confirm those six things changed and nothing else did. Two minutes.

Round 2 still has a job, just not this one — it's the document that records what was independently verified and found correct. If you keep a review-record component in the deposit, that's where it belongs, alongside the round-1 report and the response.
